paragraphs.text: These are pieces of [ripe pu’er](shou:definition) cakes from the 1980s, made from Yunnan leaf and broken over the years, now sold loose. The cakes date from the style’s first two decades: Yunnan’s state factories only brought the [wet-pile method](shou:wet-piling) into production in 1973, heaping damp leaf so its own warmth could ferment it in weeks.

At forty-one years the tea sits well within what the trade counts as [aged ripe pu’er](shou:age-aged). The leaf keeps changing slowly with the air and moisture around it, so storage has shaped these pieces as much as time has.

brewing.text: Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, deep cup with woody, date-like or medicinal notes, which the trade calls aged aroma.
